summary: TLS handshakes usually carry fairly static data such as the server certificate chain and the list of trusted certificate authorities, which can be large. This proposed standard defines a TLS extension that lets a client say it already has a cached copy, so the server can skip sending it. That makes handshakes smaller, which matters most on constrained networks and devices.

plainLanguage.summary: When you visit a friend you already know, you do not need to show your ID every time. This lets a computer say it already remembers the long paperwork, so the other side does not repeat it.

subtitle: A TLS extension that lets a client say it already has the server's certificate, so the server can send a short hash instead.

tldr.problem: TLS handshakes carry fairly static, sometimes large data such as the server certificate chain and the list of trusted CAs, which hurts on low-bandwidth, lossy networks such as IEEE 802.15.4, Bluetooth Low Energy or low power wide area networks.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a cached_info extension in its ClientHello listing fingerprints (SHA-256 hashes) of cached objects. If they are still current, the server replies with the extension and sends only the hash in place of the full Certificate or CertificateRequest message.
tldr.outcome: Handshakes get smaller when the cache is valid, and stale caches fall back to the full message. The fingerprints are sent in the clear, which can let an observer correlate exchanges.

today: RFC 7924 is a Proposed Standard from July 2016 and, per the registry metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the extension in terms of TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246).

sections.title: Shrinking the TLS Handshake
sections.content:
Cutting the data in a Transport Layer Security handshake helps where devices sit on low-bandwidth, lossy radio links, as with the Internet of Things (the RFC names IEEE 802.15.4, Bluetooth Low Energy and low power wide area networks). The server certificate can be big, especially when bundled with the intermediate CA certificates up to the root.

The typical flow is: the client and server run a full handshake and the client caches the server's certificate. Later, without using session resumption, the client connects again and attaches the cached_info extension to its ClientHello with the fingerprint of the cached certificate. If the certificate has not changed, the server does not resend the certificate or chain. If it has changed, the server sends it in full so the client can update its cache. The description applies equally to DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The first time, the server shows everything. Next time you say 'I remember it, here is its nickname', and the server skips the long show.

sections.title: The cached_info Extension
sections.content:
The extension type is cached_info(25), used in ClientHello and ServerHello. In the ClientHello its data is a CachedInformation structure: a list of 1 to 2^16-1 CachedObject entries. Each client entry has a type and a hash_value of 1 to 255 bytes. In the server's reply, each entry holds only the type. A client MAY send several objects of the same type, for example when it cached multiple certificates from a server.

Two types are defined:

  • cert (1): the client sends the fingerprint of the server's Certificate message.
  • cert_req (2): the client sends the fingerprint of the CertificateRequest message.

New hash algorithms may be added by registering new types. They MUST NOT have a collision resistance worse than SHA-256.
sections.plainLanguage: The client holds up a little tag for each thing it remembers. There are two kinds of tags: one for the server's ID card and one for the server's list of whose ID cards it accepts.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
A client MAY include the extension, and if it does it MUST list at least one CachedObject. A server that supports it MAY echo the extension in the ServerHello, which tells the client that the listed types are supported. The server MUST only list types that the client offered. For each type it lists, it MUST alter the transmission of the matching message.

The server compares the client's hash with the fingerprint of the message it would normally send. On a mismatch it MUST send the information in full and MUST NOT list that type in the extension. When a server hosts many sites, the client SHOULD use the Server Name Indication extension (RFC 6066) to pick the right cache entry.

For cert, the server MAY send a shortened Certificate message when it implements the extension, a policy enables it, and the fingerprint matches. The message then holds just hash_value. The same pattern applies to cert_req, and only when the server wants to request a client certificate. The extension is compatible with raw public keys (RFC 7250).
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the client's nickname against its own records. If it matches, it just says the nickname back. If the ID has changed, it hands over the new one.

sections.title: Fingerprint Calculation
sections.content:
The fingerprint is the SHA-256 hash (RFC 6234) of the input data, which is the Certificate or CertificateRequest message. It covers only that structure, not record-layer type or length information. The output of SHA-256 is used as is.

Its purpose is to help the server select the right information, not to carry the security of the handshake, which depends on the private key. If an attacker injects a wrong fingerprint, either it matches nothing and the server falls back to a full exchange, or it points to data the client has not cached and the exchange fails later when the signature does not verify against the client's cached public key.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint is a short code made by scrambling the whole document the same way every time, so two sides can check they mean the same document without sending it.

sections.title: Example Exchange
sections.content: In the full handshake the server sends its Certificate in the first flight, and the client stores it. In a later handshake the client adds cached_info=(cert) to its ClientHello. The server answers with cached_info=(cert) in the ServerHello, and its Certificate message now carries just the fingerprint. The rest of the handshake, from ClientKeyExchange to Finished, proceeds as usual. Appendix A of the RFC shows a hash calculation over an example certificate with a NIST P256 elliptic curve public key.
sections.plainLanguage: Round one: the server shows its whole ID. Round two: the client says 'I remember it' and the server only repeats its nickname.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Fingerprints travel in the unencrypted ClientHello and ServerHello, so an observer may be able to correlate independent TLS exchanges. Server certificates are public, but other cached types that may be defined later might not be, so deployers should decide whether this fits their privacy goals, and if worried avoid sending fingerprints in the clear.

Omitted parts are not in the handshake transcript covered by Finished, but since the fingerprints are exchanged in the early messages, they are included.

Clients MUST only cache information from legitimate sources, and only after a TLS exchange completes successfully. Otherwise an attacker could inject wrong data into the cache and mount man-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the nickname is said out loud, someone listening might notice you keep visiting the same friend. And only write a name down in your memory once you are sure it was really your friend.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA added cached_info(25) to the TLS ExtensionType Values registry and created the TLS CachedInformationType Values registry. Its entries are 0 (Reserved), 1 (cert), 2 (cert_req) and 224-255 (Reserved for Private Use). Values 0-63 need Standards Action and values 64-223 need Specification Required.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list was started so everyone agrees what number means which kind of remembered item.
